question: How do instructional qualifications and teaching preparation differ between secondary school educators and university professors?
answer: Instructional qualifications and teaching preparation differ between secondary school educators and university professors in that secondary school educators often have degrees or certifications in teaching in addition to degrees in subject matter, whereas university professors most likely have not taken a course in teaching as part of their graduate program [openstax-college-success-p31-para000]. University professors may also have additional responsibilities such as conducting research, mentoring graduate students, and serving on committees [openstax-college-success-p30-para002]. In contrast, secondary school educators may be required to complete student teaching experiences and background checks before placement in a school setting [openstax-college-success-p144-para002].

question: How does the textbook define procrastination?
answer: Procrastination is defined as the act of delaying some task that needs to be completed [openstax-college-success-p92-para000].

events.query: How does the textbook define procrastination?

results.text:
Figure 3.6 We can think of many creative ways to procrastinate, but the outcome is often detrimental. (Credit: University of the Fraser Valley / Flickr / Attribution 2.0 Generic (CC BY 2.0))
Simply put, procrastination is the act of delaying some task that needs to be completed. It is something we all
do to greater and lesser degrees. For most people, a little minor procrastination is not a cause for great
concern. But there are situations where procrastination can become a serious problem with a lot of risk. These
include: when it becomes a chronic habit, when there are a number of tasks to complete and little time, or
when the task being avoided is very important.

The Effects of Procrastination
In addition to the causes of procrastination, you must also consider what effects it can have. Again, many of
these effects are obvious and commonly understood, but some may not be so obvious and may cause other
issues. Loss of Time
The loss of time as an effect of procrastination is the easiest to identify since the act of avoiding a task comes
down to not using time wisely. Procrastination can be thought of as using the time you have to complete a
task in ways that do not accomplish what needs to be done. Loss of Goals
Another of the more obvious potentially adverse effects of procrastination is the loss of goals. Completing a
task leads to achieving a goal. These can be large or small (e.g., from doing well on an assignment to being
hired for a good job).

Because we all procrastinate from time to time, we usually do not give it much thought, let alone think about
its causes or effects. Ironically, many of the psychological reasons for why we avoid a given task also keep us
from using critical thinking to understand why procrastination can be extremely detrimental, and in some
cases difficult to overcome. To succeed at time management, you must understand some of the hurdles that may stand in your way. Procrastination is often one of the biggest. What follows is an overview of procrastination with a few
suggestions on how to avoid it. The Reasons behind Procrastination
There are several reasons we procrastinate, and a few of them may be surprising.

question: What five steps does the SQ3R reading strategy title stand for?
answer: The SQ3R reading strategy title stands for Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review [openstax-college-success-p173-para005].

events.query: What five steps does the SQ3R reading strategy title stand for?

results.text:
The SQ3R Reading Strategy
You may have heard of the SQ3R method for active reading in your early education. This valuable technique is
perfect for college reading. The title stands for Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review, and you can use the
steps on virtually any assigned passage. Designed by Francis Pleasant Robinson in his 1961 book Effective
Study, the active reading strategy gives readers a systematic way to work through any reading material. Chapter 5 Reading and Notetaking 163

They include, not always in this order:
• bringing any prior knowledge about the topic to the reading session,
• asking yourself pertinent questions, both orally and in writing, about the content you are reading,
• inferring and/or implying information from what you read,
• learning unfamiliar discipline-specific terms,
• evaluating what you are reading, and eventually,
• applying what you’re reading to other learning and life situations you encounter. Let’s break these steps into manageable chunks, because you are actually doing quite a lot when you read. Figure 5.4 The six elements of recursive reading should be considered as a circular, not linear, process.

The common nature of procrastination includes delaying tasks due to various reasons, and it can become a serious problem when it becomes a chronic habit, when there are multiple tasks to complete with little time, or when the task being avoided is very important [openstax-college-success-p92-para000].

Get Organized
Much of this chapter is dedicated to defining and explaining the nature of time management. The most
effective way to combat procrastination is to use time and project management strategies such as schedules,

one of the primary functions of setting priorities.

suggestions on how to avoid it. The Reasons behind Procrastination

results.text:
The SQ3R Reading Strategy
You may have heard of the SQ3R method for active reading in your early education. This valuable technique is
perfect for college reading. The title stands for Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review, and you can use the
steps on virtually any assigned passage. Designed by Francis Pleasant Robinson in his 1961 book Effective
Study, the active reading strategy gives readers a systematic way to work through any reading material. Chapter 5 Reading and Notetaking 163

They include, not always in this order:
• bringing any prior knowledge about the topic to the reading session,
